International Court of Justice · General List No. 192 South Africa v. Israel South Africa says Israel has been committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and in December 2023 it took Israel to the United Nations’ highest court over it. Israel says the accusation is false, and that it has been defending itself against Hamas since the attack of October 7, 2023. In 2024 the court ordered Israel three times to take steps to protect Palestinians in Gaza while the case goes on. It has not decided whether genocide happened, and that decision is years away. The two sides are still trading written arguments, and the next one is due on November 22, 2027. Filed Dec 29, 2023 Before The full court Next due Nov 22, 2027 Status Undecided

Applicant The country that brought the case Brought the case in December 2023 South Africa joined the Genocide Convention in 1998, four years after the end of apartheid. It brought this case without having been harmed itself, under a rule that lets any member of the treaty take another to court to make it keep the treaty, and the court accepted in 2024 that it can. It says it condemned Hamas’s attack on October 7, 2023, and that no attack can justify genocide. Its ambassador to the Netherlands, Vusimuzi Madonsela, is its agent in the case, and its lawyers are a team of South African, British and Irish advocates. Ronald Lamola, its justice minister at the time, opened the first hearing. Officials of the State of Palestine and the heads of three Palestinian rights groups sat with its delegation. Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶¶ 18, 33–34 · CR 2024/1 pp. 4–8, 19

Respondent The country answering it Denies the accusation Israel ratified the Genocide Convention in 1950, about two years after the state was founded and soon after the treaty was written in answer to the Holocaust. It says its war in Gaza is self-defense against Hamas and other armed groups, which killed more than 1,200 people in Israel on October 7, 2023 and took about 240 hostages. It says it has tried to limit harm to civilians and to let aid in, calls the accusation false, and has asked the court to throw the case out. Its case is run by government lawyers from the justice and foreign ministries, led in court by Tal Becker and Gilad Noam. Its first judge on the case, Aharon Barak, a former head of Israel’s Supreme Court who survived the Holocaust as a child, stepped down in June 2024. Ron Shapira, a law professor, has sat in his place since. Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶¶ 13, 18 · CR 2024/2 p. 75 · Barak opinion ¶ 4 · Order of May 21, 2026
Notes Record reviewed through October 14, 2026 . Nothing filed after that date is reflected here.
How this was made, and what it leaves out

Built from the court’s own public record of the case: South Africa’s application, the three orders of 2024 and every judge’s opinion on them, the verbatim records of the four hearings, the written requests and answers the court has published, its press releases, and its orders since. Every characterization of a side comes from that side’s own words in court or in a published filing, and every finding is quoted from the order it’s in. Each citation opens the court’s own document, at the page where one is given. The court’s website sometimes checks a browser before it hands over a file, so a link can take a moment. ICJ, case 192

Most of the case. The full written arguments, South Africa’s memorial of October 2024 and Israel’s counter-memorial of March 2026, are confidential under the court’s rules until it decides to publish them, which usually happens when the hearings on them open. So are the reports Israel has filed on how it’s carrying out the orders, and the evidence South Africa sent the court in August 2026 about whether it is. South Africa has said its memorial runs to more than 750 pages, with more than 4,000 pages of evidence behind it. Israel has said its answer shows the court has no power over the case. Beyond that, these pages can’t say what either one argues, and the Argument View quotes each side from what it said in court in 2024. DIRCO, Oct 28, 2024 · Order of May 21, 2026

Numbers here come with whose numbers they are. The court’s first order used United Nations figures that came from the health authorities in Gaza and said they “cannot be independently verified”: 25,700 Palestinians killed by January 24, 2024. The same authorities’ count passed 73,000 by August 2026, which is the number South Africa gave the court that month. For October 7, 2023, the court’s figures are more than 1,200 people killed in Israel and some 240 taken hostage. People are named here when they spoke in court, wrote an opinion, or were quoted by the court. The statements by Israeli officials quoted on these pages are the ones the court itself quoted in January 2024. Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶¶ 13, 46, 52 · DIRCO, Aug 28, 2026

Not legal advice, not a finding, and not a verdict. The court has not decided whether genocide happened. Its 2024 orders found that the rights South Africa wanted protected were plausible, which is a much lower test. Joan Donoghue, who was president of the court when it gave the first order, said afterward that “the shorthand that often appears, which is that there’s a plausible case of genocide, isn’t what the court decided.” Other bodies have looked at the war in Gaza in other ways: the International Criminal Court, which tries people, the same court’s advisory opinions, and a United Nations commission of inquiry. None of that is part of this case, and where these pages mention it they say so. Where the record doesn’t reach, these pages say so and stop. Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶¶ 30, 54 · BBC HARDtalk, Apr 25, 2024

The United Nations’ own court, in The Hague. It settles disputes between countries, not cases against people. It has 15 judges elected by the UN for nine years at a time, and it’s sometimes called the World Court.
The 1948 treaty that defines genocide and makes the countries that join it promise to prevent it and punish it. Israel joined in 1950 and South Africa in 1998.
The clause of the Genocide Convention that lets one member take another to this court over a dispute about the treaty. It’s the only reason this court has the case.
A judge a country picks for one case when no judge of its nationality is on the court. They sit and vote with the other judges.
The judge the others elect to run the court and chair its hearings, for three years at a time.
The head of the court’s staff. Keeps the record, sits with the judges at hearings, and reads out the French text of a ruling.
The official who speaks for a country in a case at this court, usually a diplomat or a government lawyer. A country can have co-agents who share the job.
Another country asking to take part. Any member of the treaty can come in to argue how the treaty should be read, and is then bound by how the court reads it. It doesn’t become a party to the case.
The court’s numbered list of its cases. This one is No. 192.
The document that starts a case at this court. South Africa’s runs to 84 pages.
The full written case of the country that sued, with its evidence. South Africa filed its in October 2024.
The full written answer of the country being sued. Israel filed its in March 2026.
A second round of writing. The country that sued answers the counter-memorial, and the other side answers that.
The court’s rules keep the written arguments out of public view until the court decides to publish them, usually when the hearings on them open.
The court’s word-for-word record of a hearing, numbered like CR 2024/1. Cited here by page.
A written decision of the court on one step in a case. It isn’t the final judgment.
Emergency orders the court can give while a case goes on, to stop harm that couldn’t be undone before the final ruling. They’re binding, but the court has no way of its own to enforce them.
The test for emergency orders. The court asks if the rights a country wants protected plausibly exist and could be at risk. It isn’t a finding that the accusation is true.
At first sight. Before giving emergency orders the court only has to see, at first sight, that it may have power over the case.
The court’s power to hear a case at all. Here it comes only from Article IX of the Genocide Convention.
A real disagreement between the two countries about the treaty. It has to exist when the case is filed. Israel argued in 2024 that there wasn’t one yet.
Whether a case the court has power over is still one it should hear, for example because of how it was brought.

A challenge to jurisdiction or admissibility filed early and decided on its own, before the main case. Israel didn’t file one. It put its objections in its counter-memorial instead, so they’re decided with everything else.
The right to bring a case. Every member of the Genocide Convention has a stake in it being kept, so any member can sue another without having been harmed itself.
The main question in a case, as opposed to steps along the way. Here, whether Israel broke the Genocide Convention.
The court’s final decision. It’s binding on the two countries and there is no appeal.
What a judge writes alongside a decision to explain a vote or add a point. A dissent explains a vote against. None of them changes the result.
Three judges the court set up in 2023 to follow whether its emergency orders are being carried out and suggest to the court what it could do.
The court said yes to the request on this card, whichever country made it.
The court ordered some of what was asked for and not the rest. It words its own orders, so they can differ from what either country asked for.
The court said no to the request on this card and ordered nothing new.

Under the treaty, any of five acts done with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group as such: killing its members, seriously harming them, imposing conditions of life meant to destroy it, preventing births, or taking its children.
The five acts in Article II of the treaty. On their own they aren’t genocide. They become genocide when an intent to destroy the group is behind them.
The intent to destroy the group as such, also called dolus specialis. It has to be there on top of the intent to do the act itself, and it’s what sets genocide apart from other crimes.
The court’s test from its earlier genocide cases. Where no plan is proved, intent can be read from a pattern of conduct only if it’s the only conclusion that could reasonably be drawn from it.
The part of the group targeted has to be big enough to matter to the group as a whole. The court said in 2024 that Palestinians in Gaza, over 2 million people, are.
Openly urging people to commit genocide. It breaks the treaty on its own, whether or not a genocide follows.
Each member has to do what it reasonably can to stop a genocide once it knows, or should know, of a serious risk of one. It’s only broken if a genocide actually happens.
This court judges countries, not people. It can find a state responsible for breaking the treaty. Putting individuals on trial is for criminal courts.

The rules for fighting a war, also called international humanitarian law. They allow some harm to civilians but forbid targeting them or causing harm out of proportion to the military aim. This case isn’t about those rules.
A country’s right to use force when it’s attacked. Israel says its war in Gaza is self-defense. South Africa says self-defense can never excuse genocide.
The worst level on the hunger scale UN agencies and aid groups use, called the IPC. It means extreme lack of food, acute malnutrition and deaths from it, each past a set line.

Where it stands Written arguments. South Africa answers Israel’s defense by November 22, 2027, and Israel answers that by May 22, 2029. Hearings and a single judgment come after that, and the judgment answers every question below the first. Either way If no If yes If yes If no If yes If no
Should the court order Israel to do anything before the case is decided?

Only about what happens while the case goes on Yes, three times · Jan, Mar and May 2024 A genocide case at this court takes years, so South Africa asked the judges for emergency orders right away, while the main question waits. The most it asked for was that Israel stop its military operations in Gaza. The test for these orders is a lot lower than proof. The court only asks if the rights South Africa wants protected are plausible, and if they’re at risk of harm that couldn’t be undone before the end of the case. The court said yes three times in 2024. In January it ordered Israel to prevent genocide, let aid in, punish public calls for genocide and keep evidence. In March, with famine setting in, it ordered aid in at scale. In May it ordered Israel to halt its offensive in Rafah, in words the judges themselves read in different ways. It never ordered a general ceasefire. None of that decides the case. The orders are binding, but the court has no police of its own. South Africa told the court in August 2026 that Israel isn’t complying, and Israel says it has kept to its obligations. Either way, the case carries on to the questions below.
Can the court hear the case at all?

The case is here Decided in the same judgment as everything else Undecided This one is about jurisdiction, which just means the court’s power to hear a case. This court can only take a case the countries involved have agreed to send it. Here the only agreement is Article IX of the Genocide Convention, which both countries joined without holding that clause back. It covers disputes about the treaty, so the court only has power over this case if it really is a dispute about genocide. In January 2024 Israel argued there wasn’t a real dispute yet when South Africa filed, because South Africa never took up its offer to talk. It also said nothing it had done could fall under the treaty. The court found enough to give its emergency orders, but it said that was only a prima facie look and not its final answer. Israel raised objections again in its answer of March 2026, on the court’s power and on whether the case should be heard at all. What they say isn’t public yet. Because Israel put them in its main answer instead of filing them early, the court will rule on them in its final judgment, along with everything else.

Outcome Then The case ends without an answer If the court decides it doesn’t have power here, the case is over and the court never says whether genocide happened. That wouldn’t clear Israel of anything. It would mean this court isn’t the one that gets to decide. The emergency orders from 2024 would end with that judgment too. This is the outcome Israel asked for in January 2024, when it asked the court to remove the case from its list.
Did Israel commit genocide in Gaza?
What the whole case comes down to

The main question Disputed This is the question people mean when they talk about the case. This court judges countries and not people, so the question is whether Israel as a state is responsible for genocide, through what its army and its officials did. That’s called state responsibility, and it’s a different thing from putting a person on trial. The court has said in earlier cases that an accusation this serious has to be proved by evidence that is “fully conclusive.” Under the treaty genocide takes two things, and they’re the two cards inside this one. Both are needed. South Africa says both are there. Israel says neither is. Who must prove it South Africa. At this court the country that makes an accusation has to prove it. Both are needed and
Were acts on the treaty’s list done to Palestinians in Gaza?

Disputed The treaty lists five acts, and the ones at the center of this case are killing members of the group, seriously harming them, and putting them in conditions of life meant to destroy them. South Africa adds measures to prevent births. These are the listed acts, and on their own they aren’t genocide yet. South Africa says the killing, the siege, the destruction of hospitals and homes, and the hunger all fit the list. Israel says the deaths and damage come from a war against Hamas fought in crowded cities where Hamas hides among civilians, and that harm to civilians in a war isn’t one of these acts. It says the right rules for that are the law of war, which this case isn’t about. The court has described the deaths, the displacement and the famine in its orders. It hasn’t decided this question.
Were they done to destroy Palestinians in Gaza as a group?

Disputed This is where most of the case will be fought. Even if the acts happened, they’re only genocide if they were done with intent to destroy the group, in whole or in part, because of who they are. The court said in 2024 that Palestinians in Gaza are a substantial part of the Palestinian people, so that piece of the test is met, at least at first sight. South Africa points to what Israeli leaders said, like a “complete siege” with “no food” and “human animals,” and to the pattern of what happened on the ground. Israel says those were random quotes that go against its actual policy, and that warning civilians to leave and letting aid in are the opposite of an intent to destroy. When there’s no written plan, the court has only accepted intent before when it was the only reasonable inference from what was done. That test is strict, and it’s being argued over in this case. The United States asked the court to keep it. Namibia argued that intent can be read from the sheer scale of what was done.

Outcome Then The court says what Israel owes The court would declare that Israel broke the treaty and is responsible for genocide. It can order Israel to stop, to punish the people responsible, and to make up for the harm, which the law calls reparation. What it can’t do is enforce that itself. If Israel didn’t comply, South Africa could go to the UN Security Council, where any of the five permanent members can block action. The judgment would still be final, and there is no appeal from it.
Did Israel break any of the treaty’s other duties?
Even if the answer above is no

The treaty’s other duties Disputed The treaty doesn’t only forbid committing genocide. It also makes every member prevent it and punish it, and punish people who publicly call for it. So a country can lose on these even if the court finds it didn’t commit genocide itself. That has happened at this court before. In 2007 it found that Serbia hadn’t committed the genocide at Srebrenica, but that it broke the treaty by failing to prevent it. The two cards inside this one are the duties South Africa says Israel failed in, and either one is enough. A yes on either one is enough or
Did it fail to prevent genocide?

Disputed Every member has a duty to prevent genocide from the moment it knows, or should know, that there’s a serious risk of one. South Africa says Israel knew at the latest when the court gave its first order in January 2024, and did too little after that. There’s a catch the court set in the Serbia case. A country only breaks this duty if a genocide actually happens. So this route only works if the court finds a genocide took place, even if not at the hands of people whose acts count as Israel’s own.
Did it fail to punish public calls for genocide?

Disputed Direct and public incitement means openly urging people to commit genocide. Unlike the others it breaks the treaty on its own, even if no genocide follows. The court ordered Israel in January 2024 to prevent and punish it, by sixteen votes to one, and Israel’s own judge voted for that order. South Africa says Israeli officials made statements like that and nobody was punished. Israel told the court in January 2024 that its attorney general had warned that calls to harm civilians may be a crime, and that several cases were being looked at. Whether anyone has been charged since isn’t in the court’s public record.

Outcome Then A finding short of genocide The court would find Israel responsible for failing in that duty, without finding that it committed genocide. That’s where Serbia ended up in 2007. The court can order Israel to put it right, and the same limits on enforcement apply as on the question above.

Outcome Then The case ends in Israel’s favor The court would find that Israel didn’t break the Genocide Convention, and its emergency orders from 2024 would end with that judgment. That still wouldn’t be a ruling that the war was lawful. Whether Israel broke the law of war is a separate question that this case can’t answer.

Every card comes from the court’s own record, or says where it comes from when it doesn’t. The full written arguments are confidential, so the cards from October 2024 on describe filings the public can’t read yet.
What the case is about, and how the two governments ended up on opposite sides of a courtroom.
Hamas leads an attack on Israel

Hamas and other armed groups from Gaza kill more than 1,200 people in Israel and take about 240 hostages, in the court’s figures. Israel goes to war in Gaza. The court’s first order describes the attack and what followed in one paragraph. Israel “launched a large-scale military operation in Gaza, by land, air and sea, which is causing massive civilian casualties, extensive destruction of civilian infrastructure and the displacement of the overwhelming majority of the population in Gaza.” Everything in this case happens against that war, and the case isn’t about the attack itself. This court can only judge countries, and Hamas isn’t a country or a party here. The court said in each of its orders that the hostages should be released “immediately and unconditionally.” Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶¶ 13–14, 85

The defense minister orders a “complete siege” of Gaza. The president says “an entire nation out there” is responsible. These words later become South Africa’s main evidence of intent. Three statements the court itself quoted in January 2024. Yoav Gallant, then defense minister, on October 9: a “complete siege” of Gaza City with “no electricity, no food, no fuel.” The next day, to troops: “We are fighting human animals.” Isaac Herzog, Israel’s president, on October 12: “It is an entire nation out there that is responsible.” Israel Katz, then energy minister, on October 13, of Gaza’s civilians: “They will not receive a drop of water or a single battery until they leave the world.” South Africa says words like these show an intent to destroy. Israel says they were “random quotes” that don’t reflect government policy, and that its cabinet decisions show what its policy really was. Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶ 52 · CR 2024/2 pp. 31–32
South Africa tells the UN Israel is breaking the treaty

At the UN General Assembly. Nine days later it writes to Israel’s embassy saying the same. South Africa’s representative said that “the events of the past six weeks in Gaza have illustrated that Israel is acting contrary to its obligations in terms of the Genocide Convention.” The note to the embassy went on December 21. These steps mattered later. This court can only hear a case if there was a real dispute between the two countries before it was filed, and the court pointed to this statement when it found one. Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶¶ 21, 26

It offers to meet. Its foreign ministry had already called the genocide accusation “wholly unfounded” and “morally repugnant.” Israel’s answering note proposed a meeting to discuss what South Africa had raised. Israel later told the court that South Africa ignored the offer and filed two days later, so there was never a real dispute between the two governments. The court disagreed. It pointed to a document Israel’s foreign ministry published on December 6, 2023, and updated later, which said the accusation was “not only wholly unfounded as a matter of fact and law, it is morally repugnant.” The court said that showed the two countries held “clearly opposite views.” Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶¶ 23, 27–28
Filed, argued and answered in four weeks.
South Africa takes Israel to the world court

Its application says Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, and asks the court to order Israel to stop its military operations at once. South Africa says Israel’s “acts and omissions” are “genocidal in character” because they’re done with the intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza as part of the wider Palestinian group. It also says Israel failed to prevent genocide and failed to punish public calls for it. It asked for nine emergency measures, and the first was that Israel “shall immediately suspend its military operations in and against Gaza.” The court can only hear the case because both countries are in the Genocide Convention, and its Article IX sends disputes about it to this court. Application ¶ 1 · Press release 2023/77 · Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶ 5

Two hours at the Peace Palace in The Hague. Its lawyers say the killing, the siege and the words of Israel’s leaders together show genocide. Its justice minister, Ronald Lamola, opened. Then Adila Hassim on the acts, Tembeka Ngcukaitobi on intent, John Dugard on the court’s power, Max du Plessis on the rights at stake, Blinne Ní Ghrálaigh on urgency and Vaughan Lowe on what the court should order. Ngcukaitobi said Israel’s leaders had “systematically and in explicit terms declared their genocidal intent” and that soldiers repeated it. The two judges ad hoc, Dikgang Moseneke for South Africa and Aharon Barak for Israel, were sworn in that morning. CR 2024/1 pp. 12–13, 20, 33

Its lawyers say South Africa told “a profoundly distorted” story, that civilian suffering in war isn’t genocide, and ask the court to throw the case out. Tal Becker opened for Israel and said that “if there have been acts that may be characterized as genocidal, then they have been perpetrated against Israel,” meaning by Hamas on October 7. Malcolm Shaw said there was “little beyond random assertions” to show an intent to destroy. Israel’s lawyers said the right rules for judging the war were the law of war, not the genocide treaty. Galit Raguan went through what Israel says it does to protect civilians and get aid in, Omri Sender argued there was no urgency, and Christopher Staker took South Africa’s nine requests one by one. Gilad Noam closed by asking the court to reject the request and to remove the case from its list. CR 2024/2 pp. 13, 15, 31, 75
The court orders six measures, and no ceasefire

Israel must take every measure in its power to prevent genocide in Gaza, let aid in, and punish public calls for genocide. The court doesn’t order the military operation to stop. The first two measures passed 15 to 2 and the ones on aid and incitement 16 to 1, because Israel’s own judge, Aharon Barak, voted for those two. Judge Sebutinde of Uganda voted against all six. Israel also had to report back within a month. This is the order most often misquoted. The court found that the Palestinians’ right to be protected from genocide was plausible, which is the test for emergency orders. It said in the same order that it was “not required to ascertain whether any violations” had happened, and that such a finding comes only at the end of the case. Order of Jan 26, 2024 ¶ 86 · ¶¶ 30, 54 · Barak opinion ¶ 44
South Africa came back three times in four months, and the court answered three different ways.

Five judges join the court and Nawaf Salam becomes its president. One of the new judges is South African, so South Africa’s judge ad hoc steps down. The new judges were Dire Tladi of South Africa, Sarah Cleveland of the United States, Juan Manuel Gómez Robledo of Mexico and Bogdan Aurescu of Romania, and Hilary Charlesworth of Australia was elected again. Judges Donoghue, Gevorgian, Bennouna and Robinson left. A country only gets a judge ad hoc if no judge of its own is on the court, so Dikgang Moseneke stopped sitting. Israel’s, Aharon Barak, stayed. Order of May 24, 2024 ¶ 6 · Order of Mar 28, 2024 p. 3

Israel is preparing an offensive on Rafah, at Gaza’s southern edge, where more than a million displaced people are sheltering. South Africa wrote to the court asking it to use its power to act on its own initiative, without waiting for a new formal request. South Africa, Feb 12, 2024 · Order of Mar 28, 2024 ¶ 6
Israel calls the case an abuse of the court

Its written answer says the accusation is “wholly unfounded” and that it is meeting its obligations whatever the court does. Israel wrote that the case “is wholly unfounded in fact and law, morally repugnant, and represents an abuse both of the Genocide Convention and of the Court itself,” and that its commitment to the law “is unwavering and applies” to the war “independently of any proceeding before the Court.” Israel, Feb 15, 2024 ¶¶ 2–3, as quoted in the US declaration ¶ 13
No new orders, but Rafah is covered

By letter, with no hearing. The January measures apply “throughout the Gaza Strip, including in Rafah,” the court says, and Israel has to carry them out. The court quoted the UN Secretary-General, who had said the developments in Rafah “would exponentially increase what is already a humanitarian nightmare.” It said this “perilous situation demands immediate and effective implementation” of the January order. Press release 2024/16 · Order of Mar 28, 2024 ¶ 7

On what it has done to carry out the January order. Like all its reports since, it isn’t public. South Africa sent the court its comments on the report on March 11. Israel filed a second report on April 29, 2024, after the March order, and its lawyer told the court in May that Israel had been “forthcoming” in both. Order of May 24, 2024 ¶¶ 9, 12 · CR 2024/28 p. 21
South Africa says Gaza is starving

It asks for new orders without a hearing, saying children are dying of hunger because of what Israel is doing. South Africa wrote that “Palestinian children are starving to death as a direct result of the deliberate acts and omissions of Israel,” including Israel’s efforts to cut off UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees. It asked the court to decide without a hearing, because of “the extreme urgency of the situation,” and the court did. South Africa, Mar 6, 2024 ¶ 8 · Press release 2024/21 · Order of Mar 28, 2024 ¶ 16
Israel says the hunger isn’t its doing

It rejects “in the strongest terms” that children are starving because of what it has done, and asks the court not to order anything new. Israel said food insecurity in Gaza, especially in the north, was “a serious challenge,” but that the fighting and the hunger were both already there when the court ruled in January. It pointed to a sea route and floating pier, air drops and aid by land, and to its work with UN agencies. It said the challenges of getting aid in were “inherent to any theatre of active hostilities, particularly one that is densely populated and heavily dependent on international aid.” Israel, Mar 15, 2024 · Order of Mar 28, 2024 ¶¶ 17, 29, 33

The court orders Israel to let aid in “at scale” and open more land crossings. That one is unanimous, and Israel’s own judge votes for it. The court said Palestinians in Gaza “are no longer facing only a risk of famine,” and that at least 31 people, 27 of them children, had died of malnutrition and dehydration, in UN figures. It ordered Israel to ensure “the unhindered provision at scale” of food, water, fuel, medical care and more, and to make sure its military doesn’t block aid. It said it couldn’t order a ceasefire by everyone, because Hamas and other countries aren’t parties to the case. This order came by letter, with no hearing. Order of Mar 28, 2024 ¶¶ 21, 44, 51 · Press release 2024/26

South Africa’s full case is due by October 28, 2024, and Israel’s answer by July 28, 2025. From here the main case runs mostly on paper. The two full written arguments are called the memorial and the counter-memorial, and both are confidential until the court decides otherwise. Colombia asked to join the case the same day. Order of Apr 5, 2024 · Order of May 21, 2026 p. 2 · Press release 2024/27

After ordering about 100,000 people out of eastern Rafah the day before. By May 18 the UN counts nearly 800,000 displaced from the city. These are the court’s own figures, taken from UN reports. Israel told the court these were “specific, limited and localized operations prefaced with evacuation efforts,” not a large-scale assault, and that Rafah was also “a military stronghold for Hamas.” Order of May 24, 2024 ¶¶ 28, 25 · CR 2024/28 p. 11
South Africa asks the court to stop the Rafah offensive

Its fourth request. It calls Rafah the “last refuge” in Gaza and asks for Israel to withdraw. South Africa said Israel now controlled every way in and out of Gaza, and that the assault on Rafah was “deliberately inflicting on Palestinians conditions of life” meant to destroy them. It asked for access for investigators and journalists too. The court called a hearing for the following week. Israel asked for it to be moved a week later, because its lawyers couldn’t get there in time, and the court said no. South Africa, May 10, 2024 ¶ 11 · Order of May 24, 2024 ¶¶ 23, 15
South Africa: “a new and horrific stage”

Its second hearing, an afternoon session. One judge, Peter Tomka, isn’t on the bench for either day. The same team as in January, minus the minister. Its agent, Vusimuzi Madonsela, said Israel’s genocide “has just reached a new and horrific stage,” and Tembeka Ngcukaitobi called Rafah “the last stand.” The court’s president opened by saying that “for reasons made known to me, Judge Tomka is unable to be present on the Bench for the duration of these hearings.” He didn’t sit for the May order either. CR 2024/27 pp. 8, 12, 42

Two government lawyers and no outside counsel. Israel says its chosen team couldn’t come on four days’ notice. Gilad Noam said Israel’s lead counsel was “shipborne this week” and that the short notice hurt “the fundamental principle of equality of arms.” He called the case “an inversion of reality” and said: “Calling something a genocide, again and again, does not make it genocide.” At the end Judge Nolte asked Israel about conditions in the zones it was sending people to, especially Al-Mawasi, and how it would get them food, water and shelter. Israel answered in writing the next day, and South Africa commented on the answer. CR 2024/28 pp. 8–9, 30 · Israel’s answer, May 18, 2024 · South Africa’s comments, May 20, 2024

Israel must “immediately halt its military offensive” in Rafah, in a sentence its own judges read in different ways. Thirteen to two. The full measure reads: “Immediately halt its military offensive, and any other action in the Rafah Governorate, which may inflict on the Palestinian group in Gaza conditions of life that could bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part.” Israel was also told to keep the Rafah crossing open and to let UN investigators into Gaza. Judge Aurescu, who voted for it, called the wording “somehow unclear.” He and Judge Nolte, who also voted for it, read it as stopping the offensive only as far as it risks those conditions of life, and the two judges who voted against read it the same way. Israel’s national security adviser said the next day, “We did not commit genocide and we will not commit genocide,” and its army kept operating in Rafah. Order of May 24, 2024 ¶ 57 · Aurescu declaration ¶ 3 · Nolte declaration ¶ 25 · Barak dissent ¶ 1 · Reporting: Times of Israel, May 25, 2024
Other countries ask to join, Israel’s judge changes, and the same court rules on the occupation in a separate case.

The State of Palestine asks to take part, both as a country with its own stake in the case and to argue how the treaty should be read. A country that isn’t a party can ask to intervene. Palestine invoked both routes the court’s Statute allows. Nicaragua had been the first to ask, in January 2024, and withdrew in April 2025. Officials of the State of Palestine sat with South Africa’s delegation at the first hearing. Palestine, Jun 3, 2024 · Press release 2024/52 · Press release 2024/14 · Press release 2025/15

Aharon Barak steps down for personal reasons, and Israel names Ron Shapira, a law professor, in his place. Barak, a former president of Israel’s Supreme Court, had written in January about surviving the Kaunas ghetto as a child, and that “I was appointed by Israel; I am not an agent of Israel.” He resigned in early June 2024, citing family reasons. Shapira, the rector of a college near Tel Aviv, has sat on the case since and was on the bench for its 2026 order. Barak opinion ¶¶ 4, 49 · Reporting: Times of Israel, Jun 6, 2024 · Reporting: Times of Israel, Jul 1, 2024 · Order of May 21, 2026 p. 2
A separate opinion on the occupation

The same court, in a different proceeding, says Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory is unlawful. It isn’t part of this case. This was an advisory opinion, which is the court’s answer to a legal question from the UN General Assembly, not a ruling in a dispute between two countries. It was about the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza since 1967. It doesn’t decide anything about genocide, and it isn’t binding the way a judgment is. The two proceedings are separate. ICJ, case 186
The arguments go in on paper, and stay private until the hearings.
South Africa files its full case

Its memorial: more than 750 pages, it says, with over 4,000 pages of evidence. Under the court’s rules nobody else can read it yet. South Africa’s government said the memorial shows Israel “promoting the destruction of Palestinians living in Gaza,” by killing them, depriving them of aid and imposing conditions of life aimed at their destruction, and defying the court’s orders. That is South Africa’s description of its own filing. The court hasn’t published it. DIRCO, Oct 28, 2024 · Order of May 21, 2026 p. 2
Arrest warrants at a different court

The International Criminal Court issues warrants for Israel’s prime minister and former defense minister. That court tries people, and it isn’t part of this case. Judges there found reasonable grounds to believe Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant were responsible for the war crime of starvation as a method of warfare and for crimes against humanity. The warrants don’t charge genocide. A warrant was also issued for Mohammed Deif, a Hamas commander. This court, the International Court of Justice, judges countries and can’t try anyone. The two courts are both in The Hague and are often confused. ICC, Nov 21, 2024

Nawaf Salam leaves the court in January to become Lebanon’s prime minister. The judges elect Yuji Iwasawa of Japan in his place. Two more seats changed hands in 2025. Mahmoud Hmoud of Jordan took Salam’s seat in May, and Phoebe Okowa of Kenya took Abdulqawi Yusuf’s in November. Julia Sebutinde, who voted against every measure in this case, has been vice-president since February 2024. Order of May 21, 2026 p. 2

Its answer, due in July 2025, is pushed to January 12, 2026. In October the president extends it again, to March 12, 2026. Israel asked both times, and the second extension was given by the court’s president. Altogether Israel’s answer came about seven and a half months after the first deadline. Order of Apr 14, 2025 · Order of Oct 20, 2025 · Order of May 21, 2026 p. 3 · DIRCO, Mar 2026

The global hunger monitor the UN relies on finds famine in Gaza City. Israel rejects the finding. It isn’t a ruling in this case. The monitor, called the IPC, is a partnership of UN agencies and aid groups. It was the first famine it had confirmed in the Middle East. Israel’s foreign ministry said, “There is no famine in Gaza,” and its prime minister called the report “an outright lie.” In December 2025 four UN agencies said famine had been pushed back, and warned the gains could be reversed. Whether hunger in Gaza was caused on purpose is one of the questions this court will have to answer. This finding is about how bad it was, not who caused it. UN monthly bulletin, Aug 2025 · FAO, UNICEF, WFP and WHO, Dec 19, 2025 · Reporting: Al-Monitor, Aug 22, 2025

An inquiry set up by the UN Human Rights Council concludes Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Israel calls the report fake. It isn’t part of this case. The commission, chaired by the South African judge Navi Pillay, found that Israeli forces committed four of the five acts the treaty lists, and that statements by officials and a pattern of conduct showed an intent to destroy. Israel didn’t cooperate with it, and its ambassador in Geneva called the report “scandalous” and “fake.” This court isn’t bound by what the commission found and will weigh the evidence itself. UN Commission of Inquiry, Sept 16, 2025 · Reporting: Geneva Solutions, Sept 16, 2025

Israel’s army pulls back to a line inside Gaza, and the hostages still alive there are released three days later. The killing goes on at a lower level. A year later the UN human rights office had verified more than 1,000 deaths in Gaza since the ceasefire was announced, and Gaza’s health ministry counted more than 1,400. Israel’s forces still hold about half of the territory or more. The ceasefire doesn’t end the case. South Africa says the court’s orders still bind Israel, and that it isn’t complying with them. UN Human Rights, Oct 2026 · UN Secretary-General, Oct 2025
Israel files its answer, and objects to the court’s power

Its counter-memorial. Israel says it shows the court has no power over the case and South Africa’s claims should be dismissed in their entirety. The court’s own summary says the answer is “voluminous,” and that besides the main case it contains “objections to the jurisdiction of the Court and the admissibility of the Application.” Israel put those objections in its main answer and didn’t file them early as preliminary objections, so they’ll be decided together with everything else. Israel’s foreign ministry called the case a “fabricated and politicized blood libel” and said Israel had “affirmed, through words and deeds, that it was targeting Hamas and its accomplices, not Gaza’s civilian population.” Order of May 21, 2026 p. 3 · Israel MFA, Mar 14, 2026
The United States joins on Israel’s reading

One of 22 countries, plus Palestine, to ask to intervene. It calls the genocide allegations “false.” Countries can join to argue how the treaty should be read. The US asked the court to keep its strict test for intent and said that “civilian casualties, even widespread civilian casualties, are not necessarily probative of genocidal intent.” Namibia, filing the same day, argued that intent can be read from the scale and repetition of the acts. Hungary, Fiji, Paraguay, the Netherlands and Iceland filed that month too. In all, 23 asked to join between January 2024 and March 2026: Nicaragua, Colombia, Libya, Mexico, Palestine, Spain, Türkiye, Chile, the Maldives, Bolivia, Ireland, Cuba, Belize, Brazil, the Comoros, Belgium, Paraguay, the Netherlands, Iceland, Namibia, the United States, Hungary and Fiji. Nicaragua and Colombia have since withdrawn. The court hasn’t yet ruled on whether the others are let in. United States ¶¶ 5, 21 · Namibia · Press release 2026/5 · Press release 2026/6
The sides meet the court’s president

South Africa wants a second round of writing and at least 18 months to prepare. Israel says one round is enough. South Africa pointed to how big Israel’s answer was and to the objections in it. Israel’s deputy agent said a second round wasn’t necessary, but that if there was one, Israel wanted the same 18 months for its own reply. Order of May 21, 2026 p. 3

South Africa’s reply is due November 22, 2027, and Israel’s rejoinder May 22, 2029. Hearings come after that. The order gave each side the 18 months it had asked for. South Africa will have to answer Israel’s objections to the court’s power in its reply. Nothing in the order sets a date for hearings or a judgment. Order of May 21, 2026 p. 3
South Africa says Israel is defying the orders

It sends a “substantial dossier” to the three judges who watch whether the court’s emergency orders are followed. It isn’t public. The court set up this monitoring committee in 2023. South Africa’s government said “Israel has not complied with the Orders,” and gave the death toll as at least 73,407 Palestinians killed and 174,335 injured by August 2026, figures from Gaza’s health authorities. The committee works in private, and the court hasn’t announced anything about the dossier. DIRCO, Aug 28, 2026

Its new government withdraws the declaration Colombia filed in April 2024. The court announces it on September 22. Colombia had filed to join under the previous president, Gustavo Petro. The government of Abelardo de la Espriella, which took office in August 2026, withdrew it. Leaving doesn’t change Colombia’s membership of the Genocide Convention. Press release 2026/24 · Colombia One, Sept 21, 2026

Did Israel intend to destroy Palestinians in Gaza as a group?

South Africa Yes. Israel’s leaders said so “in explicit terms,” soldiers repeated it on the ground, and the pattern of what was done fits it. The evidence is “overwhelming and incontrovertible.” Israel No. The quotes are “random assertions” that go against government policy.
